newsitem.title: USA: EPA plan for muni landfills draws industry fire.
newsitem.headline: EPA plan for muni landfills draws industry fire.

text.p: Industry groups on Monday slammed an EPA plan to cap local communities' liability for Superfund toxic waste cleanup costs at landfills they operated.
Under the proposal, municipalities that owned and operated landfills would be responsible for no more than 20 percent of total cleanup costs at Superfund sites which they had run.
EPA said it wanted to ensure that parties who only sent household trash or similar waste to municipal landfills would not be held liable for cleaning up toxic waste.

"The second goal is to provide a fair and efficient mechanism to deal with the liability of municipalities who owned or operated landfills as part of their obligation to provide basic waste disposal services to their citizens," EPA said.

Oil, chemical and insurance industry officials said the proposal would undermine talks to overhaul the Superfund program, in which they are pressing to ease liability for all polluters and make the government pick up more of the tab.
"We need total reform, not a piecemeal approach," said a spokesman for the American Petroleum Institute.

Although they had not all evaluated EPA's proposal yet, industry groups said if EPA favored selected parties, such as municipal landfill owners, those parties would have no incentive to help work out a new Superfund program.
"Why wouldn't private landfills with the same mix of waste get the same treatment?" said Tom Gilroy, a spokesman for the Chemical Manufacturers Association.
Critics also raised concern that if some parties were let off the hook for their share of payments, those remaining would have an unfair burden.
"We're always worried if you start carving people out, there will not be many people left to take care of the program," Gilroy said.
An insurance industry official predicted that if the proposal was applied to specific Superfund sites and was then challenged, EPA was likely to lose in court.
"Courts have not looked very kindly on this selective, differential regulatory enforcement," said David Pratt, a senior vice president of the American Insurance Association.
